```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(Lahman)
```

## Lesson goals

In this lesson, we use Major League Baseball batting data to learn how
principal component analysis (PCA) can summarize many related
quantitative variables.

## 1. Baseball in simple terms

Baseball is a game between two teams. One team bats and tries to score
runs; the other team fields and tries to record outs. A batter can reach
base by getting a hit, receiving a walk, or being hit by a pitch. The
batter and other runners advance around four bases. Reaching home plate
scores a run.

An individual player-season is one player's statistics for one year. The
Lahman data may contain several rows for a player in the same year if
the player changed teams. We combine those rows so each analysis row
represents one player in one season.

## 2. Offensive statistics in simple terms

### Counting statistics

Counting statistics record how many times an event happened. Examples
include:

- `H`: hits
- `HR`: home runs
- `R`: runs scored
- `RBI`: runs batted in
- `BB`: walks
- `SB`: stolen bases

Counting statistics are strongly affected by playing time. A player who
plays 162 games usually has more hits than an equally productive player
who plays 60 games.

### Rate statistics

Rate statistics divide an event by an opportunity. They help us compare
players who had different amounts of playing time.

- `BA` (batting average) = hits divided by at-bats
- `OBP` (on-base percentage) = times reaching base divided by the
  selected denominator
- `SLG` (slugging percentage) = total bases divided by at-bats
- `HR_rate` = home runs divided by plate appearances

PCA works well here with rates because we want to study how players
produced, rather than simply how long they played.

## PCA concepts: what PCA does

PCA is a way to replace many related variables with a smaller number of
new variables called principal components.

Imagine that we measure a player using several batting rates. Many of
those rates are correlated: players with high home-run rates may also
have high slugging percentages and RBI rates. PCA looks for a new
direction through the data that captures as much variation as possible.

### A simple two-variable example

Suppose we measure only two characteristics:

- power: a player's home-run tendency;
- contact: a player's ability to get hits.

If these two variables tend to increase together, the first component
might look approximately like:

$$PC1 = 0.70(\text{power}) + 0.70(\text{contact})$$

This component measures a general offensive dimension: players high in
both variables receive high PC1 scores.

The second component might look approximately like:

$$PC2 = 0.70(\text{power}) - 0.70(\text{contact})$$

This component contrasts power with contact. A player with much more
power than contact will score high on PC2, while a player with much more
contact than power will score low on PC2.

The exact coefficients are calculated by PCA. The coefficients are
called loadings, and the score for one player is found by multiplying
the player's standardized variables by those loadings and adding the
results.

```{r}
example_data <- tibble(
  power = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
  contact = c(1.2, 2.1, 2.8, 4.2, 5.1)
)

example_pca <- prcomp(
  example_data,
  center = TRUE,
  scale. = TRUE
)

example_pca$rotation
example_pca$x

# The two loading vectors are orthogonal.
sum(example_pca$rotation[, 1] * example_pca$rotation[, 2])
```

The final value is approximately zero. That is how we can see the
orthogonality of the two component directions.

### Why do we center and scale?

Centering subtracts the mean from every variable:

$$x_{\text{centered}} = x - \bar{x}$$

After centering, each variable has an average of zero. PCA then
describes how observations vary around the center of the data.

Scaling divides each centered variable by its standard deviation:

$$x_{\text{scaled}} =
\frac{x - \bar{x}}{\text{standard deviation}(x)}$$

After scaling, each variable has a standard deviation of one.

This matters because batting variables are measured on different scales.
For example, BA is usually between 0 and 1, while HR_rate is much
smaller and RBI_rate may have a different spread. Without scaling, a
variable with the largest numerical spread could dominate PCA simply
because of its units.

In this lesson, scale. = TRUE means that prcomp() centers and scales the
original rates before calculating the components. Later, we create
z-scores within each year. Those variables are already standardized
within year, so we do not scale them a second time.

### Why are the components orthogonal?

PCA chooses PC1 first, pointing in the direction that explains the most
variation. PC2 is then chosen to explain as much of the remaining
variation as possible while being perpendicular to PC1. Additional
components continue this process.

Orthogonality means the components are uncorrelated in the data used to
fit the PCA. It does not mean that the original batting statistics are
unrelated. In fact, PCA is useful partly because the original variables
are related.

Each component is a linear combination of all the variables included in
the analysis:

$$PC1 = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + \cdots + w_px_p$$

The rotation matrix shows the weights (w) or loadings. The x matrix in
the PCA result contains each player-season's coordinates, called scores,
on those new axes.

## 3. Load the baseball data

The `Lahman` package contains historical Major League Baseball data.
Install the packages once if they are not already installed.

```{r}
# Install once if needed:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "Lahman"))

library(tidyverse)
library(Lahman)

glimpse(Batting)
```

## 4. Create one row per player-season

We identify the counting statistics that should be added when a player
played for more than one team during the same year.

```{r}
counting_variables <- c(
  "G", "AB", "R", "H", "X2B", "X3B", "HR",
  "RBI", "SB", "CS", "BB", "SO", "IBB",
  "HBP", "SH", "SF", "GIDP"
)

batting_season <- Batting |>
  filter(yearID >= 1900) |>
  group_by(playerID, yearID) |>
  summarize(
    across(
      all_of(counting_variables),
      ~ sum(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(AB >= 200)
```

The `AB >= 200` filter gives us players with a substantial number of
at-bats. It reduces the chance that a few plate appearances create
extreme rates.

## 5. Add player position

`Batting` does not contain a simple primary-position variable. The
`Fielding` table records positions, so we select the position with the
most fielding appearances for each player-season.

```{r}
player_position <- Fielding |>
  filter(yearID >= 1900) |>
  group_by(playerID, yearID, POS) |>
  summarize(
    fielding_games = sum(G, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  group_by(playerID, yearID) |>
  slice_max(fielding_games, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  transmute(
    playerID,
    yearID,
    Position = POS
  )

batting_season <- batting_season |>
  left_join(player_position, by = c("playerID", "yearID")) |>
  mutate(Position = replace_na(Position, "Unknown"))
```

Some players may have multiple positions or no recorded fielding
position. This lesson assigns the position with the most fielding
appearances.

## 6. Create plate appearances and batting rates

We use this approximation for plate appearances:

$$PA = AB + BB + HBP + SH + SF$$

We calculate traditional rates and event rates per plate appearance.

```{r}
batting_season <- batting_season |>
  mutate(
    PA = AB + BB + HBP + SH + SF,

    # Traditional rates
    BA = H / AB,
    OBP = (H + BB + HBP) / (AB + BB + HBP + SF),
    SLG = (H + X2B + 2 * X3B + 3 * HR) / AB,

    # Uncomment if you want OPS in the analysis.
    # OPS = OBP + SLG,

    # Event rates per plate appearance
    R_rate = R / PA,
    X2B_rate = X2B / PA,
    X3B_rate = X3B / PA,
    HR_rate = HR / PA,
    RBI_rate = RBI / PA,
    SB_rate = SB / PA,
    BB_rate = BB / PA,
    SO_rate = SO / PA

    # Optional variables. Add a comma after SO_rate if enabling these:
    # ,CS_rate = CS / PA
    # ,IBB_rate = IBB / PA
    # ,HBP_rate = HBP / PA
    # ,SH_rate = SH / PA
    # ,SF_rate = SF / PA
    # ,GIDP_rate = GIDP / PA
  ) |>
  filter(if_all(where(is.numeric), is.finite))
```

The commented-out variables are optional choices. PCA is affected by
which variables we include, so those choices should be documented.

## 7. Choose the variables for PCA

We carry along identifying variables separately. They identify players
and help us interpret PCA results, but they are not used to calculate
the components.

```{r}
rate_variable_names <- c(
  "BA", "OBP", "SLG",
  "R_rate", "X2B_rate", "X3B_rate",
  "HR_rate", "RBI_rate", "SB_rate",
  "BB_rate", "SO_rate"
)

analysis_data <- batting_season |>
  left_join(
    People |>
      transmute(
        playerID,
        player_name = paste(nameFirst, nameLast)
      ),
    by = "playerID"
  ) |>
  select(
    any_of(c("playerID", "player_name", "yearID", "Position")),
    all_of(rate_variable_names)
  )

analysis_data |>
  select(any_of(c("playerID", "player_name", "yearID", "Position"))) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

## 8. Run PCA using the original rates

PCA finds new axes that are weighted combinations of the original
variables. PC1 explains the greatest amount of variation; PC2 explains
the greatest remaining amount, subject to being perpendicular to PC1.

Because the variables use different scales, we center and standardize
them inside `prcomp()`.

```{r}
rate_variables <- analysis_data |>
  select(all_of(rate_variable_names)) |>
  select(where(~ sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE) > 0))

pc_rates <- prcomp(
  rate_variables,
  center = TRUE,
  scale. = TRUE
)

summary(pc_rates)
pc_rates$rotation
```

The `rotation` table contains the loadings. A large positive loading
means the variable contributes positively to a component. A large
negative loading means it contributes in the opposite direction. The
sign of a PCA component is arbitrary: multiplying an entire component by
-1 describes the same pattern.

```{r}
rate_scores <- as_tibble(pc_rates$x) |>
  bind_cols(
    analysis_data |>
      select(any_of(c("playerID", "player_name", "yearID", "Position")))
  )

rate_scores |>
  select(any_of(c("player_name", "yearID", "Position", "PC1", "PC2"))) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

ggplot(rate_scores, aes(PC1, PC2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.30) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "MLB Player-Seasons Using Batting-Rate PCA",
    x = "Principal Component 1",
    y = "Principal Component 2"
  )
```

## 9. Normalize rates within each baseball year

Baseball changes over time. Rules, equipment, training, ballparks,
player populations, and strategies can all change. A batting average or
home-run rate from 1920 should not automatically be compared with the
same raw rate from 2000.

To compare players with the players of their own era, we calculate a
z-score within each year:

$$z = \frac{\text{player rate} - \text{year average}}{\text{year standard deviation}}$$

A value of 2 means the player was about two within-year standard
deviations above that year's average for that statistic.

```{r}
within_year_z <- function(x) {
  x_mean <- mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  x_sd <- sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)

  if (is.na(x_sd) || x_sd == 0) {
    rep(0, length(x))
  } else {
    (x - x_mean) / x_sd
  }
}

z_rate_data <- analysis_data |>
  group_by(yearID) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      all_of(rate_variable_names),
      within_year_z,
      .names = "z_{.col}"
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

z_rate_variable_names <- paste0("z_", rate_variable_names)

z_rate_variables <- z_rate_data |>
  select(all_of(z_rate_variable_names)) |>
  select(where(~ sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE) > 0))

pc_z_rates <- prcomp(
  z_rate_variables,
  center = TRUE,
  scale. = FALSE
)

summary(pc_z_rates)
pc_z_rates$rotation

z_rate_scores <- as_tibble(pc_z_rates$x) |>
  bind_cols(
    z_rate_data |>
      select(any_of(c("playerID", "player_name", "yearID", "Position")))
  )
```

Because the rates have already been standardized within year, we do not
scale them again. We still center the columns overall before calculating
PCA.

```{r}
ggplot(z_rate_scores, aes(PC1, PC2, color = yearID)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.40) +
  scale_color_viridis_c() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Era-Normalized Batting PCA",
    subtitle = "Each rate is standardized relative to its own baseball year",
    x = "Principal Component 1",
    y = "Principal Component 2",
    color = "Year"
  )
```

## 10. Add Hall of Fame status

Hall of Fame status is not used as an input to PCA. It is a label used
to examine whether Hall of Fame players occupy different parts of PCA
space.

```{r}
hof_players <- HallOfFame |>
  filter(inducted == "Y") |>
  distinct(playerID)

z_rate_scores <- z_rate_scores |>
  mutate(
    HOF = if_else(
      playerID %in% hof_players$playerID,
      "Hall of Fame",
      "Not Hall of Fame"
    )
  )

table(z_rate_scores$HOF)

ggplot(z_rate_scores, aes(PC1, PC2, color = HOF)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Era-Normalized PCA by Hall of Fame Status",
    x = "Principal Component 1",
    y = "Principal Component 2",
    color = "Status"
  )
```

### Optional: run a separate PCA using Hall of Fame player-seasons

This is different from coloring the same PCA by Hall of Fame status. The
PCA below is calculated using only Hall of Fame players, so its axes
should not be directly compared with the all-player axes.

```{r}
hof_z_data <- z_rate_data |>
  filter(playerID %in% hof_players$playerID)

hof_z_variables <- hof_z_data |>
  select(all_of(z_rate_variable_names)) |>
  select(where(~ sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE) > 0))

pc_hof <- prcomp(
  hof_z_variables,
  center = TRUE,
  scale. = FALSE
)

summary(pc_hof)
pc_hof$rotation

hof_scores <- as_tibble(pc_hof$x) |>
  bind_cols(
    hof_z_data |>
      select(any_of(c("playerID", "player_name", "yearID", "Position")))
  )

ggplot(hof_scores, aes(PC1, PC2, color = Position)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "PCA Using Hall of Fame Player-Seasons Only",
    x = "Hall of Fame PC1",
    y = "Hall of Fame PC2",
    color = "Position"
  )
```

## 11. Compare PC1 and PC2 by year and position

The following charts show how the PCA space changes over time and how
different positions are distributed in that space.

```{r}
ggplot(z_rate_scores, aes(PC1, PC2, color = yearID)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35) +
  facet_wrap(~ Position) +
  scale_color_viridis_c() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Era-Normalized PCA by Year and Position",
    x = "PC1",
    y = "PC2",
    color = "Year"
  )

ggplot(z_rate_scores, aes(x = Position, y = PC1, fill = Position)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE, outlier.alpha = 0.15) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "PC1 Distribution by Position",
    x = "Position",
    y = "PC1"
  )

ggplot(z_rate_scores, aes(x = Position, y = PC2, fill = Position)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE, outlier.alpha = 0.15) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "PC2 Distribution by Position",
    x = "Position",
    y = "PC2"
  )
```

### Position centers in PCA space

This plot shows the average PC1 and PC2 score for each position. It is a
summary; it does not mean every player at that position is similar.

```{r}
position_centers <- z_rate_scores |>
  group_by(Position) |>
  summarize(
    mean_PC1 = mean(PC1, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_PC2 = mean(PC2, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(position_centers, aes(mean_PC1, mean_PC2, label = Position)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray80") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "gray80") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(nudge_y = 0.12, check_overlap = TRUE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Average PCA Location by Position",
    x = "Average PC1",
    y = "Average PC2"
  )
```

## 12. Find extreme and near-zero player-seasons

The largest PC score is not automatically the best player. It means that
the player-season has a strong positive value on that component. We need
the loadings to understand what the component represents.

Here, closest to zero means closest to zero on one component. It does
not mean the player was average in every individual statistic.

```{r}
get_pc_examples <- function(data, component, n = 20) {
  scores <- data |>
    select(
      any_of(c("playerID", "player_name", "yearID", "Position", "HOF")),
      all_of(component)
    ) |>
    rename(score = all_of(component))

  list(
    highest = scores |>
      arrange(desc(score)) |>
      slice_head(n = n) |>
      mutate(category = "Highest"),

    lowest = scores |>
      arrange(score) |>
      slice_head(n = n) |>
      mutate(category = "Lowest"),

    closest_to_zero = scores |>
      mutate(distance_from_zero = abs(score)) |>
      arrange(distance_from_zero) |>
      slice_head(n = n) |>
      select(-distance_from_zero) |>
      mutate(category = "Closest to zero")
  )
}

pc1_examples <- get_pc_examples(z_rate_scores, "PC1", n = 20)
pc2_examples <- get_pc_examples(z_rate_scores, "PC2", n = 20)

all_pc_examples <- bind_rows(
  pc1_examples$highest |> mutate(component = "PC1"),
  pc1_examples$lowest |> mutate(component = "PC1"),
  pc1_examples$closest_to_zero |> mutate(component = "PC1"),
  pc2_examples$highest |> mutate(component = "PC2"),
  pc2_examples$lowest |> mutate(component = "PC2"),
  pc2_examples$closest_to_zero |> mutate(component = "PC2")
) |>
  select(
    component,
    category,
    any_of(c("player_name", "playerID", "yearID", "Position", "HOF")),
    score
  )

all_pc_examples
```

For example, the six individual tables are available as follows:

```{r}
pc1_examples$highest
pc1_examples$lowest
pc1_examples$closest_to_zero

pc2_examples$highest
pc2_examples$lowest
pc2_examples$closest_to_zero
```

## 13. How to interpret this analysis

PCA is primarily an exploratory and dimensionality-reduction method. It
can help us:

- summarize many correlated batting variables with two or three
  components;
- visualize player-seasons in a two-dimensional chart;
- identify players with similar statistical profiles;
- discover which statistics move together;
- create compact predictors for a later model.

PCA does not prove that a player is better, does not establish
causation, and does not guarantee that PC1 has a meaningful baseball
interpretation. Inspect the loadings, compare explained variance, and
use baseball knowledge to interpret the patterns.

## 14. Salary and PC1 comparison

The Lahman package includes a Salaries table beginning in 1985. A player
can have more than one salary record in a season if the player changed
teams, so we add those records to obtain one total salary per
player-season.

We use the latest season available in both the batting and salary data.

```{r}
last_season <- min(
  max(batting_season$yearID),
  max(Salaries$yearID)
)

last_season
```

```{r}
salary_by_season <- Salaries |>
  filter(yearID == last_season) |>
  group_by(playerID, yearID) |>
  summarize(
    salary = sum(salary, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

salary_scores <- bind_rows(
  rate_scores |>
    filter(yearID == last_season) |>
    select(playerID, player_name, yearID, Position, PC1) |>
    mutate(model = "Original-rate PCA"),
  z_rate_scores |>
    filter(yearID == last_season) |>
    select(playerID, player_name, yearID, Position, PC1) |>
    mutate(model = "Era-normalized PCA")
) |>
  left_join(salary_by_season, by = c("playerID", "yearID")) |>
  filter(!is.na(salary), salary > 0) |>
  mutate(log_salary = log10(salary))

salary_scores
```

Salary is strongly right-skewed, so the graph uses a logarithmic salary
axis. This makes it easier to see players at both the low and high ends.

```{r}
ggplot(salary_scores, aes(salary, PC1, color = model)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = paste("PC1 and Salary in", last_season),
    subtitle = "Salary is shown on a logarithmic scale",
    x = "Total annual salary",
    y = "PC1",
    color = "PCA model"
  )
```

We can calculate a correlation for each model. Because a correlation is
sensitive to outliers, it is useful to compare the ordinary correlation
with the correlation between PC1 and log salary.

```{r}
salary_correlations <- salary_scores |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    correlation_salary = cor(PC1, salary, use = "complete.obs"),
    correlation_log_salary = cor(PC1, log_salary, use = "complete.obs"),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

salary_correlations
```

This is an association, not evidence that PCA scores cause salaries.
Salary also reflects playing time, position, age, experience, team
finances, negotiating history, injuries, and many other factors. The PCA
score is based only on the batting rates selected earlier.

## 15. Compare top and bottom PC1 player-seasons

The original-rate PCA compares raw rate patterns across the entire
historical period. The era-normalized PCA compares each player with the
players from the same year. Therefore, the top player in the second
model represents someone who was especially strong relative to that
player's era.

```{r}
get_pc1_extremes <- function(data, model_name, n = 20) {
  bind_rows(
    data |>
      arrange(desc(PC1)) |>
      slice_head(n = n) |>
      mutate(category = "Top PC1"),
    data |>
      arrange(PC1) |>
      slice_head(n = n) |>
      mutate(category = "Bottom PC1")
  ) |>
    mutate(model = model_name) |>
    select(
      model,
      category,
      any_of(c("player_name", "playerID", "yearID", "Position", "HOF")),
      PC1
    )
}

pc1_original_extremes <- get_pc1_extremes(
  rate_scores,
  "Original-rate PCA"
)

pc1_z_extremes <- get_pc1_extremes(
  z_rate_scores,
  "Era-normalized PCA"
)

pc1_comparison <- bind_rows(
  pc1_original_extremes,
  pc1_z_extremes
)

pc1_comparison
```

To focus only on the top and bottom five from each model:

```{r}
pc1_comparison |>
  group_by(model, category) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  ungroup()
```

Interpret the results using the loadings:

- A top PC1 player has a strong positive combination of the statistics
  with positive PC1 loadings.
- A bottom PC1 player has a strong negative combination of those
  statistics.
- A top player in the era-normalized model was especially unusual
  compared with that player's contemporaries.
- The two models may identify different players because the original
  model is influenced by differences between baseball eras.

## 16. Salary, PC1, and possible value

This section uses salary as a rough measure of how highly the player was
valued by their team. It is not a perfect measure of player quality.
Salary is also affected by experience, contracts, position, injuries,
and the player's reputation.

The first table shows the highest-paid player-seasons in the latest
season available. It lists PC1 from both models:

- Original-rate PCA: compares the player's rates across all seasons.
- Era-normalized PCA: compares the player's rates with other players in
  the same season.

```{r}
highest_salary_players <- salary_scores |>
  arrange(desc(salary)) |>
  group_by(model) |>
  slice_head(n = 20) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(
    model,
    player_name,
    playerID,
    yearID,
    Position,
    salary,
    PC1
  )

highest_salary_players
```

A player with a high salary but a low PC1 score may be an established
player who had a below-average season. A low PC1 score does not prove
that the player was bad overall; it describes that player-season
relative to the variables and comparison group used in the PCA.

```{r}
high_salary_low_pc1 <- salary_scores |>
  filter(PC1 < 0) |>
  arrange(desc(salary)) |>
  group_by(model) |>
  slice_head(n = 20) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(
    model,
    player_name,
    playerID,
    yearID,
    Position,
    salary,
    PC1
  )

high_salary_low_pc1
```

Now we look for possible high-performing, lower-paid player-seasons. The
threshold PC1 \> 2.2 identifies player-seasons with unusually high PC1
scores. We then sort those player-seasons from lowest salary to highest
salary.

```{r}
low_salary_high_pc1 <- salary_scores |>
  filter(PC1 > 2.2) |>
  group_by(model) |>
  arrange(salary, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 20) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(
    model,
    player_name,
    playerID,
    yearID,
    Position,
    salary,
    PC1
  )

low_salary_high_pc1
```

These are not automatically bargains. A strong PC1 score may reflect
only the batting statistics included in this analysis. A complete
salary-value analysis would also consider playing time, defense,
baserunning, age, injuries, contract year, and future performance.
